The other day I heard the term "civil inattention" on the radio. They explained it briefly without giving it much attention. I don’t remember what they were talking about, but they simply used it to support an argument that I no longer recall.

Civil inattention is the polite way of handling interactions with strangers without establishing any interpersonal communication or feeling the need to respond to contact from a stranger. Goffman (1963) used the example of an elevator to explain this phenomenon. Inside the elevator, a person does not look at, speak to, or touch the person next to them; however, if there are many people inside the elevator, it is possible that they are close enough to touch each other, but even in this case, each person maintains an impassive behavior so as not to affect anyone around them.

In other words, we act as if others do not exist to respect their privacy and their right to individuality. The curious thing is that to courteously ignore the presence of others, say, in a train car, we must start from the premise that they are there and, therefore, acknowledge their presence. It seems like a contradiction, but I find it an act of extreme civilization and refined education, to esteem the respect of others so much as to make the "sacrifice" of deciding to ignore them. It’s not something bad or detached as it may seem at first glance; it is supremely polite.

This doesn’t mean that human relationships are affected; on the contrary, it offers the possibility of establishing bonds with strangers. Brief, veiled, and silently agreed-upon bonds; a gentleman’s agreement.

I mean to say that courteous inattention is not pretending that the other person does not exist, which is what we often encounter while walking down the street or on public transport. There are heartless people who run over those in front of them, forget the priority seats in train cars, and play music at high volume to the obvious horror of the other passengers. This is diametrically opposed to the concept of courteous inattention. It means, "I know you are there, I know I could bother you with some of my actions, but I absolutely don’t care." In some cases, it even seems that the more rejection they provoke among the people around them, the more they enjoy it.

I was taught courteous inattention as a child, though it wasn’t called that; I was simply told to "be polite." Something as simple as that. I can’t help but wonder why those values are no longer being passed down. One reason that comes to mind, which I can understand, is living in extreme economic hardship; that is, when the basics are missing (food, shelter...), the first thing to go is the more "superficial" elements like good manners. I haven’t found myself in such a situation, and I hope it remains that way forever, but I suppose that if you barely have enough to fill your plate, it doesn’t matter if you rest your elbows on the table. Just eat what you can and eat quickly.

What this leads to is a dumbing down of society and further separation of the classes. I immediately think these conclusions are not accidental, that there is a certain interest in this happening. Who could benefit from the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer? Exactly.

But it’s not just about keeping us poor, or even in a state of "apparent well-being," the goal is to keep us ignorant, narrow-minded, and poorly educated. So when the classes clash, they can always be scandalized and say, "pearls before swine." Well, you’re right, they aren’t for swine.

In one of my physics classes, I was taught that behavior on a small or microscopic scale closely resembles behavior on a larger or higher level. For example, the distribution of water molecules when it boils. The molecules spread out as far from each other as possible until there’s no more room. This is exactly how people behave when they enter an empty subway car. Everyone sits as far away from each other as possible. For instance, if out of a group of four seats, two are occupied, you won’t take the third seat if there’s another group of four seats completely free. You’ll sit alone in the group of four. This behavior is repeated constantly, and it’s easy to observe how in a few seconds, people choose their seat by quickly glancing around the car and locating the seat with the least "population density." Until, indeed, the spaces run out, even standing, and courteous inattention comes into play, leading to ridiculous situations. One can be completely pressed against another person and try to lift a hand to read a newspaper folded into three parts (because unfolded it wouldn’t fit in any way), and glance sideways at the pages as if nothing is happening. As if one could ignore that their cheek is pressed against a stranger’s chest. But that’s how we cope, by ignoring it.

Because the opposite would be quite chaotic. In Japan, these concepts are taken to the extreme, and people walk down the street looking at the ground, avoiding the annoying contact with others. It’s not that they’re made of different stuff, or special, it’s that the opposite would be chaos. Japan is a mega-city where people can take a magnetic train that travels six hundred kilometers in an hour to get to work every day. It’s like someone living in Madrid and working in Barcelona every day. This happens in Japan; the surface area is so vast and the population so large that their society rests on the pillars of education. Imagine those giant pedestrian crossings with eternal traffic lights where everyone goes wherever they please, running, walking slowly, with loud music, bumping into each other. Everything would fall apart in no time. I repeat, everything would fall apart in no time.
